text: A single qubit's state can't be fully captured by a probability bar chart alone — two different states can give identical measurement probabilities but point in completely different directions in a deeper geometric sense. The Bloch sphere is the standard way to see that extra information.

Theta, the polar angle, controls how close a state is to zero versus one. Phi, the azimuthal angle, controls the relative phase between the two amplitudes, information a plain probability bar chart throws away entirely, since P-zero and P-one only depend on theta, never on phi. You can compute Bloch coordinates directly from raw amplitudes without ever going through theta and phi explicitly. And Matplotlib's mplot3d toolkit draws a wireframe sphere plus an arrow, with quiver, for the state vector itself.

Four landmark states anchor the whole picture. Ket-zero sits at the north pole, zero, zero, one. Ket-one sits at the south pole, zero, zero, negative one. The plus state, zero plus one over root two, sits on the equator at one, zero, zero. And the plus-i state sits on the equator too, but at zero, one, zero, a different point even though it has the exact same fifty-fifty measurement probabilities as plus.

Starting from alpha equals beta equals one over root two, z equals abs alpha squared minus abs beta squared gives zero. x, built from alpha times the conjugate of beta, gives one. y gives zero. This is exactly the plus state, landing at one, zero, zero, confirming the raw-amplitude formula agrees with the theta-phi table.

fig dot add_subplot with projection equals 3d is the key line that turns ax into a 3D axes object. set_box_aspect of one, one, one keeps the sphere from looking stretched into an egg shape. And ax dot quiver draws the state as a crimson arrow from the origin out to its x, y, z point.

Next lesson's lab puts this whole chapter together: computing measurement probabilities, turning them into expected shot counts for a real experiment, and plotting the result as the histogram-style bar chart you'll see in the output of almost every real quantum circuit run.
